claim: Prokaryotic mechanosensitive (MS) channels open by sensing the physical state of the membrane.
source: Prokaryotic mechanosensitive (MS) channels open by sensing the physical state of the membrane.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract describing the basic mechanism of MS channels, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The cryo-EM structures of E. coli MscS in nanodiscs reveal a novel membrane-anchoring fold.
source: Here, we describe cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the E. coli small-conductance mechanosensitive channel (MscS) in nanodiscs (ND). They reveal a novel membrane-anchoring fold that plays a significant role in channel activation
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data obtained from cryo-EM experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The cryo-EM structures establish a new location for the lipid bilayer, shifted ~14 Å from previous consensus placements.
source: They reveal a novel membrane-anchoring fold that plays a significant role in channel activation and establish a new location for the lipid bilayer, shifted ~14 Å from previous consensus placements.
evidence: This is supported by direct measurements from the cryo-EM density maps comparing the new structure to previous models.

claim: A phospholipid 'hooks' the top of each TM2-TM3 hairpin and likely plays a role in force sensing.
source: A phospholipid that 'hooks' the top of each TM2-TM3 hairpin and likely plays a role in force sensing
evidence: This is based on observed lipid density in the cryo-EM structure, with functional interpretation based on location and interactions.

claim: A bundle of acyl chains occludes the permeation path above the L105 cuff.
source: and a bundle of acyl chains occluding the permeation path above the L105 cuff.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM density maps showing lipid-like density in the pore region.

claim: Mechanosensitive channels couple force sensing with the electrical activity of cells.
source: Many of these functions are driven by the activity of mechanosensitive channels, switches that couple force sensing with the electrical activity of cells (Cox et al., 2018; Naismith and Booth, 2012; Perozo, 2006; Sukharev and Corey, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work in the field.

claim: When the membrane is stretched, the resulting change in the trans-bilayer pressure profile drives the conformational equilibrium of membrane proteins.
source: When the membrane is stretched, the resulting change in the trans-bilayer pressure profile will drive the conformational equilibrium of membrane proteins (Cantor, 1999; Gullingsrud and Schulten, 2004).
evidence: This is a mechanistic principle supported by cited theoretical and computational studies.

claim: MscL and MscS are the foundational members of two structurally distinct classes of MS channels in prokaryotes.
source: In prokaryotes, MscL and MscS are the foundational members of two structurally distinct classes of MS channels (Cox et al., 2018; Kung et al., 2010; Naismith and Booth, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: MscL and MscS are sensitive to tension changes in the plane of the bilayer.
source: Sensitive to tension changes in the plane of the bilayer, they play a key role in the response to osmotic challenges
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanosensitivity mechanism of these channels.

claim: The E. coli MscS crystal structure revealed a homoheptamer with three TM segments (TM1, TM2 and TM3a/b) and a large cytoplasmic C-terminal domain.
source: The E. coli MscS crystal structure in detergent (Bass et al., 2002; Steinbacher et al., 2007) revealed a homoheptamer with three TM segments (TM1, TM2 and TM3a/b) and a large cytoplasmic C-terminal domain cradling a water-filled internal cavity.
evidence: This describes the architecture determined from previous crystal structures, supported by citations.

claim: The narrowest region along the permeation path in MscS is located at L105 in TM3a.
source: The narrowest region along the permeation path is located at L105 in TM3a
evidence: This is a structural feature identified from crystal structures and confirmed in the current work.

claim: The current consensus is that the original MscS crystal structure represents a non-conductive conformation.
source: and while its van der Waals diameter can be larger than 7 Å, the current consensus is that the original crystal structure represents a non-conductive conformation (Anishkin et al., 2010).
evidence: This represents the field's interpretation of the crystal structure, supported by citation.

claim: Whether the original MscS crystal structure corresponds to a closed or an inactivated state has been a matter of discussion.
source: However, whether it corresponds to a closed or an inactivated state has been a matter of discussion (Anishkin and Sukharev, 2004; Anishkin et al., 2008a; Anishkin et al., 2008b).
evidence: This acknowledges ongoing debate in the field, supported by citations to different perspectives.

claim: Structures believed to represent a conducting or expanded state have been obtained for the gain of function mutant A106V.
source: Structures believed to represent a conducting or expanded state have been obtained for the gain of function (GOF) mutant A106V (Wang et al., 2008)
evidence: This refers to previously published structural work on a mutant form of MscS.

claim: Structures believed to represent a conducting or expanded state have been obtained in DDM-solubilized wt-MscS.
source: and in DDM-solubilized wt-MscS (Lai et al., 2013).
evidence: This refers to previously published structural work on wild-type MscS in detergent.

claim: The transition to the expanded state in MscS appears to be associated with rearrangements in the packing interface between TM3 helices.
source: A comparison with wt-MscS revealed that transition to this expanded state appears to be associated with rearrangements in the packing interface between TM3 helices.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison of different crystal structures.

claim: Crystallographically-derived conformational changes in MscS are in general agreement with lower resolution analyses of amphiphile-driven gating in a lipid bilayer.
source: These crystallographically-derived conformational changes (in detergent) are in general agreement with lower resolution analyses of amphiphile-driven gating of MscS in a lipid bilayer (Vasquez et al., 2008).
evidence: This compares structural findings with functional studies, supported by citation.

claim: Early hypotheses suggested that membrane lateral forces at the aqueous interface disrupt the hydrophobic interactions between TM1-TM2 hairpin.
source: Early hypotheses suggested that membrane lateral forces at the aqueous interface (Nomura et al., 2006) disrupt the hydrophobic interactions between TM1-TM2 hairpin, straightening the tilt angle of TM3a and TM3b and opening the channel (Anishkin et al., 2008b; Vasquez et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes a previously proposed mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: At rest, internal elastic strain energy might be countered by the bilayer pressure profile, keeping the channel closed.
source: Alternatively, at rest, internal elastic strain energy might simply be countered by the bilayer pressure profile, keeping the channel closed (Anishkin et al., 2008b; Malcolm et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes an alternative proposed mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: A unique mechanism has been proposed based on the idea that bilayer lipids can drive MscS conformation by acting as ligands while they freely exchange between the membrane and hydrophobic pockets between TM2 and TM3a.
source: More recently, a unique mechanism has been proposed based on the idea that bilayer lipids can drive MscS conformation by acting as ligands while they freely exchange between the membrane and hydrophobic pockets between TM2 and TM3a (Pliotas et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a recently proposed mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: According to the lipid-as-ligand model, at rest, TM2/TM3a pockets are saturated with phospholipids, preventing structural rearrangements in TM3a.
source: At rest, these pockets are saturated with phospholipids, preventing structural rearrangements in TM3a.
evidence: This describes a component of the previously proposed lipid-as-ligand mechanism.

claim: According to the lipid-as-ligand model, as tension is applied, lipids diffuse away from TM2/TM3a pockets, leading to TM3a movements and opening the channel.
source: But as tension is applied, lipids diffuse away, leading to TM3a movements and opening the channel.
evidence: This describes the proposed mechanism of channel opening in the lipid-as-ligand model.

claim: The lipid-as-ligand model requires that the TM2/TM3a cavity must be located at the membrane/water interface.
source: This model requires not only that the TM2/TM3a cavity must be located at the membrane/water interface
evidence: This is a stated requirement of the previously proposed mechanism.

claim: Until recently, all available high-resolution MscS structures have been determined in detergent micelles.
source: Yet, until recently (Rasmussen et al., 2019), all available high-resolution structures have been determined in detergent micelles, either by crystallographic (Bass et al., 2002; Dong et al., 2015; Lai et al., 2013; Pliotas et al., 2015; Steinbacher et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2008) or single particle cryo-EM methods (Guo and MacKinnon, 2017; Saotome et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the history of structural studies, supported by multiple citations.

claim: A recent EM structure of MscS in a nanodisc showed lipids in the TM2-TM3 hairpin cavity, two lipids parallel to TM3b, and a putative lipid density along the permeation pathway.
source: However, in a recent EM structure of MscS in a nanodisc (Rasmussen et al., 2019), lipids were observed in the TM2-TM3 hairpin cavity, two lipids parallel to TM3b, and a putative lipid density was reported along the permeation pathway.
evidence: This describes findings from a recently published structure, supported by citation.

claim: The structure of nanodisc-reconstituted MscS (PC:PG, 4:1) with a histidine tag at its N-terminal end was determined to a resolution of 3.1 Å.
source: We first determined the structure of nanodisc-reconstituted MscS (PC:PG, 4:1) with a histidine tag at its N-terminal end (6xHis-MscS-ND) to a resolution of 3.1 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of the resolution achieved in the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The MscS-ND structure shows a slightly different angle for the TM1-TM2 hairpin compared to the crystal structure.
source: While the EM structure (Figure 1A) recapitulates some of the major characteristic seen in the MscS crystal structure (Bass et al., 2002; Steinbacher et al., 2007), the channel shows a slightly different angle for the TM1-TM2 hairpin
evidence: This is based on comparison of the new structure with previous crystal structures.

claim: The MscS-ND structure displays additional density towards its periplasmic face corresponding to a newly resolved N-terminal domain.
source: and displays additional density towards its periplasmic face. This is a consequence of a newly resolved N-terminal domain and additional ~3 turns of helix that further extends TM1 in MscS-ND (Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This describes new structural features observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: The newly resolved N-terminal domain and the lower end of the TM1-TM2 hairpin represent the most flexible regions of the channel.
source: This domain displays some anisotropic behavior, and together with the lower end of the TM1-TM2 hairpin, they represent the most flexible regions of the channel (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density and resolution maps.

claim: The N-terminal ring in MscS is potentially stabilized by both polar (E2-Q11) and hydrophobic (van der Waals) (L23-L24, Y27-V29) interacting pairs at the inter-subunit interface.
source: The N-terminal ring is potentially stabilized by both polar (E2-Q11) and hydrophobic (van der Waals) (L23-L24, Y27-V29) interacting pairs at the inter-subunit interface (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM model identifying specific residue interactions.

claim: W16 sits deep in a pocket at the bottom of the N-terminal domain.
source: Conserved residues (in blue) are predominantly found at the subunit interface, while W16 sits deep in a pocket at the bottom of the N-terminal domain.
evidence: This describes the structural location of a specific residue in the model.

claim: Tryptophan residues have been shown to be enriched at the membrane interface and contribute about ~4 kcal/mol as 'anchors' of TM segments in membranes.
source: Indeed, tryptophan residues have been shown to be enriched at the membrane interface and contribute about ~4 kcal/mol as 'anchors' of TM segments in membranes (de Jesus and Allen, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about tryptophan residues in membrane proteins, supported by citation.

claim: The MscS N-terminal domain is named the 'anchor' domain based on its membrane placement and location of the conserved W16.
source: Given its membrane placement and location of the conserved W16, we named the MscS N- terminal the 'anchor' domain.
evidence: This is a naming decision based on structural and functional inference.

claim: Other than the upper third of TM1 and anchor domain, the structure of MscS-ND is rather similar to the MscS crystal structure in detergent (2OAU) with ~1.4 Cα RMSD.
source: Strikingly, other than the upper third of TM1 and anchor domain the structure of MscS-ND is rather similar to the MscS crystal structure in detergent (2OAU) (Steinbacher et al., 2007) (~1.4 Cα RMSD, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is based on quantitative structural comparison between the new and previous structures.

claim: Previous attempts to reconfigure the interactions between TM2 and TM3 to compensate for perceived low inter-helical packing are not supported by the present data.
source: Previous attempts to reconfigure the interactions between TM2 and TM3 to compensate for perceived low inter-helical packing (Anishkin et al., 2008a; Vásquez et al., 2008) are not supported by the present data.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of the new structure with previously proposed models.

claim: The present EM structure represents the physiological closed state of MscS.
source: In fact, we reason that the present EM structure represents the physiological closed state: The channel is at rest, embedded in a lipid bilayer and ostensibly, in the absence of any applied tension.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental conditions and structural features.

claim: Clear density corresponding to the oligomeric assembly of individual Hisx6 tags is observed as a 'crown' on top of MscS.
source: Furthermore, as MscS-ND includes a 6xHis tag at the N-terminus (with a 10 residue linker), clear density corresponding to the oligomeric assembly of individual Hisx6 tags is observed as a 'crown' on top of MscS (Figure 2A left, Figure 3, left and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a specific feature observed in the cryo-EM density.

claim: The His-tag crown leads to the formation of a strong stabilizing force, which precludes N-terminal movement in the closed state.
source: This crown leads to the formation of a strong stabilizing force, which precludes N-terminal movement in the closed state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation and subsequent functional data.

claim: 6xHis-MscS-ND appears insensitive to mechanical stimulation in HEK293 cells patch-clamp experiments under high-speed pressure clamp conditions.
source: 6xHis-MscS-ND appears insensitive to mechanical stimulation in HEK293 cells patch-clamp experiments under high-speed pressure clamp conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data from patch-clamp experiments.

claim: Functional inhibition of 6xHis-MscS-ND is fully relieved upon in situ thrombin treatment.
source: This functional inhibition is fully relieved upon in situ thrombin treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data showing recovery of function after proteolytic cleavage.

claim: The anchor domain must move away from its current position upon channel opening.
source: strongly suggesting that the anchor domain must move away from its current position upon channel opening, in a way consistent with the MscS expanded conformation (Lai et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data and comparison with expanded structures.

claim: The nanodisc lipid bilayer in MscS-ND is upwards shifted ~14 Å when compared to the previous consensus placement.
source: Remarkably, our data show that the disc-like region corresponding to the nanodisc lipid bilayer (Figure 2A B left) is upwards shifted ~14 Å when compared to the previous consensus placement (Figure 2B, center).
evidence: This is based on direct measurement from the cryo-EM density.

claim: The membrane not only interacts closely with the N terminal domain but a large portion of the cytoplasmic end of the TM1-TM2 hairpin and most of TM3a (including the location of the vapor lock) now lies outside of the membrane.
source: Given this location, the membrane not only interacts closely with the N terminal domain (Figures 1A,B,2A) but a large portion of the cytoplasmic end of the TM1-TM2 hairpin and most of TM3a (including the location of the vapor lock) now lies outside of the membrane
evidence: This is a direct consequence of the revised membrane placement observed in the structure.

claim: The revised membrane arrangement is fully compatible with the distribution of MscS surface charged residues.
source: This arrangement is fully compatible with the distribution of MscS surface charged residues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the charge distribution in relation to the membrane position.

claim: Modern algorithmic predictions of membrane placement are in agreement with the present membrane location when the MscS-ND structure is evaluated.
source: Furthermore, modern algorithmic predictions of membrane placement (Lomize et al., 2012; Newport et al., 2019) are in agreement with the present membrane location when the MscS-ND structure is evaluated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is based on computational predictions using established algorithms, supported by citations.

claim: PMF calculation reveals a clear energy minima centered precisely at the location experimentally defined by the EM density.
source: Calculation of the free energy as a function of linear displacement reveals a clear energy minima centered precisely at the location experimentally defined by the EM density (Figure 2C, left).
evidence: This is based on computational free energy calculations using molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Equilibration of three bilayer positions (upwards and downwards of MscS-ND placement) all converge to the EM density position within 60 ns.
source: Indeed, equilibration of three bilayer positions (upwards and downwards of MscS-ND placement) all converge to the EM density position within 60 ns (Figure 2C, right).
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The contribution of hydrophobic mismatch dominates that of membrane curvature in determining membrane position.
source: When the free energy change based on our continuum calculation is compared to those obtained from PMF calculations, the contribution of hydrophobic mismatch dominates that of membrane curvature (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis comparing different energetic contributions.

claim: The same bilayer placement is observed in MscS-ND structures with and without N-terminal 6xHis.
source: Figure 3 shows that the same bilayer placement is observed in the EM densities for two PC:PG MscS-ND structures (with and without N-terminal 6xHis, Figure 3—figure supplements 1,3)
evidence: This is based on comparison of multiple independently determined structures.

claim: The same bilayer placement is observed in nanodiscs containing E. coli polar lipids.
source: and in nanodiscs containing E. coli polar lipids (at 10 Å resolution), suggesting that MscS-bilayer placement is not affected by alternative lipid compositions.
evidence: This is based on structural determination in different lipid compositions.

claim: The EM density in DDM appears to show a similar placement for the detergent micelle.
source: The EM density in DDM (at about 3.4 Å, Figure 3—figure supplements 2,3) appears to show a similar placement for the detergent micelle.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure determined in detergent.

claim: The structure of the N-terminal domain has partially unraveled in DDM.
source: However, the structure of the N-terminal domain has partially unraveled (Figure 3, red arrow), suggesting a rationale for why this region is unresolved under crystallographic conditions or in nanodiscs in the absence of the N-terminal 6xHis (Rasmussen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on observation of the DDM structure and comparison with other conditions.

claim: Seven clearly defined phospholipids appear to 'hook' the top of each of the TM2-TM3 loops.
source: Notably, we find lipid-like densities both, in a newly defined cavity between subunits and at the center of the permeation pathway (Figure 5A). Seven clearly defined phospholipids appear to 'hook' the top of each of the TM2-TM3 loops
evidence: This is based on observation and modeling of lipid density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The hook lipids are firmly embedded by threading their head group through an inter-subunit opening formed by the extended TM1 and the top of the TM2-TM3 hairpin.
source: The hook lipids are firmly embedded by threading their head group through an inter-subunit opening formed by the extended TM1 and the top of the TM2-TM3 hairpin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B) and facing the permeation path.
evidence: This describes the structural arrangement of the hook lipids based on the cryo-EM model.

claim: Binding of the hook lipids is stabilized by R88 in one subunit and Y27 from the neighboring subunit.
source: Indeed, binding of the hook lipids is stabilized by R88 in one subunit and Y27 from the neighboring subunit (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM model identifying specific interactions.

claim: Both R88 and Y27 are known to generate LOF phenotypes when mutated.
source: Both residues are known to generate LOF phenotypes when mutated (Figure 4D; Rasmussen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on previous functional studies, supported by citation and data in the current manuscript.

claim: A cluster of seven linear densities is observed lining the patch of hydrophobic residues immediately above the narrowest region of the permeation pathway (L105).
source: A cluster of seven linear densities is also observed lining the patch of hydrophobic residues immediately above the narrowest region of the permeation pathway (L105) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This describes observed density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The pore lipids are hypothesized to be either acyl chains from a fairly mobile phospholipid or perhaps bound fatty acids trapped along the permeation pathway.
source: Although there is no clear indication of EM density associated with headgroups (whether it is PE or PG), we hypothesize these are either acyl chains from a fairly mobile (and not fully resolved) phospholipid or perhaps bound fatty acids trapped along the permeation pathway.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed density characteristics.

claim: The pore lipids are stabilized (likely weakly) via hydrophobic interactions along TM3.
source: Modeled as hexadecanes, the pore lipids are stabilized (likely weakly) via hydrophobic interactions along TM3 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and analysis of interactions.

claim: A tryptophan scan encompassing TM3a and the TM2-TM3 linker shows a remarkable correlation with LOF residues aligning at the putative hook lipid binding pocket and the pore lipids interaction surface.
source: Interestingly, a tryptophan scan encompassing TM3a and the TM2-TM3 linker (Rasmussen et al., 2015) shows a remarkable correlation with LOF residues aligning at the putative hook lipid binding pocket and the pore lipids interaction surface (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structure with previous functional mutagenesis data.

claim: The pore and hook lipids were carried over from the cell membrane during purification and reconstitution.
source: We believe the pore and hook lipids were carried over from the cell membrane during purification and reconstitution, as we find evidence of similarly placed density in our DDM MscS map (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on observation of lipid density in both nanodisc and detergent structures.

claim: An evaluation of the electron density map for the 2OAU crystal structure displays unassigned density that precisely corresponds to the location of the phosphate group in the hook lipid.
source: Furthermore, an evaluation of the electron density map for the 2OAU crystal structure (Steinbacher et al., 2007) displays unassigned density that precisely corresponds to the location of the phosphate group in the hook lipid (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B), implying unresolved lipid-bound density in MscS crystals.
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of previously published crystallographic data.

claim: Non-denaturing mass spectroscopy identified at least five phospholipids per MscS (mostly PE).
source: And while MS and chemical extraction helped identify at least five phospholipids per MscS (mostly PE) the predicted placement and interaction with MscS (Pliotas et al., 2015) appears to be incompatible with those observed in the present EM densities (Figure 5).
evidence: This refers to previous mass spectrometry data, supported by citation.

claim: The EM density does not show explicit lipid density in the TM2-TM3 pockets.
source: Our EM density does not show explicit lipid density in the TM2-TM3 pockets.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: Lipids bound to the TM pockets have been reported recently in ND-reconstituted MscS.
source: However, lipids bound to the TM pockets have been reported recently in ND-reconstituted MscS (Rasmussen et al., 2019), but whether or not these lipids play a functional role remains to be established.
evidence: This refers to findings from a recent publication, supported by citation.

claim: In spite of a wide (~7 Å) diameter at rest, the hydrophobic characteristics of the pore lead to a functional occlusion by a 'vapor lock' mechanism.
source: Previous studies of closed state water permeation in MscS (Anishkin and Sukharev, 2004; Spronk et al., 2006) have shown that in spite of a wide (~7 Å) diameter at rest, the hydrophobic characteristics of the pore lead to a functional occlusion by a 'vapor lock' mechanism.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous computational studies, supported by citations.

claim: During a 10 ns MD run, the running averages for water permeation in the absence of bound lipid fluctuates around two water molecules in a 3 × 2 Å cylinder centered at L105.
source: Figure 6A shows that during a 10 ns MD run the running averages for water permeation in the absence of bound lipid fluctuates around two water molecules in a 3 × 2 Å cylinder centered at L105.
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Inclusion of the hook lipid atop the TM2-TM3 hairpin reduces the running average to about one water molecule at a time.
source: Inclusion of the hook lipid atop the TM2-TM3 hairpin reduces the running average about one water molecule at a time.
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data comparing different conditions.

claim: The addition of both hook and pore lipids thoroughly eliminates any water permeability.
source: However, the addition of both hook and pore lipids thoroughly eliminates any water permeability.
evidence: This is based on molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: Under physiological conditions the pore lipid might be able to act as a low dielectric blocker.
source: The substantial effect of the pore lipid on water dynamics further suggests that under physiological conditions the pore lipid might be able to act as a low dielectric blocker
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results showing the effect on water permeation.

claim: The transition to the open conformation in MscS could be accompanied by a reduction in the occupancy of the pore lipid along the permeation pathway.
source: suggesting that the transition to the open conformation in MscS could be accompanied by a reduction in the occupancy of the pore lipid along the permeation pathway.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed effects of the pore lipid on water permeation.

claim: TM3b can no longer be considered an interfacial helix as it is located almost 15 Å away from the membrane/water interface.
source: For one, TM3b can no longer be considered an interfacial helix (Bavi et al., 2016b) as it is located almost 15 Å away from the membrane/water interface (Figures 1A,2B, left).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the revised membrane placement in the structure.

claim: The proposed gating mechanisms where lipids act as ligands are unlikely due to the location of the TM2/TM3a cavity in relation to the membrane annulus around MscS.
source: The proposed gating mechanisms where lipids act as ligands are based on the assumption that the TM2/TM3a cavity is open and accessible to the lipid bilayer (Pliotas et al., 2015) are unlikely due to the location of the TM2/TM3a cavity (or TM pocket) in relation to the membrane annulus around MscS (Figure 2B) seems incompatible with a proposed phospholipid exchange between bilayer and TM pockets.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural data contradicting a previously proposed mechanism.

claim: The suggestion that lateral tension would 'pull' on lipid acyl chains located in TM pockets appears unrealistic.
source: Accordingly, the suggestion that lateral tension would 'pull' on lipid acyl chains located in TM pockets appears unrealistic.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural findings regarding membrane placement.

claim: The anchor domain is unusually sensitive to mutagenesis with up to 70% of its amino acids leading to LOF (or severe GOF) phenotypes upon mutation to ALA.
source: finally, we show that the anchor domain is unusually sensitive to mutagenesis with up to 70% of its amino acids leading to LOF (or severe GOF) phenotypes upon mutation to ALA (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on systematic alanine scanning mutagenesis data.

claim: Deletion of the anchor domain renders MscS unresponsive to tension, although it does not preclude its folding and oligomeric assembly.
source: First, deletion of the anchor domain renders MscS unresponsive to tension, although it does not preclude its folding and oligomeric assembly (Figures 2A,4B)
evidence: This is based on functional and structural characterization of the deletion mutant.

claim: Limiting the conformational flexibility of the anchor domain by the N-terminal His-x6 'bundle' leads to non-functional MscS.
source: second, limiting the conformational flexibility of the anchor domain by the N-terminal His-x6 'bundle' leads to non-functional MscS
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data showing loss of function.

claim: Deleting the His-x6 'bundle' via proteolysis restores activity to WT level.
source: and deleting the His-x6 'bundle' via proteolysis restores activity to WT level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D)
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data showing recovery of function.

claim: Changes in NiEdda accessibility between closed and open MscS conformations show a massive reduction in water accessibility for the majority of the anchor domain.
source: Changes in the NiEdda (water) accessibility between closed (at rest, in liposomes) and open MscS conformations (after LysoPC activation) show a massive reduction in water accessibility for the majority of the anchor domain (Figure 7A) when compared to the values at rest (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on previous EPR spectroscopy data, supported by citation.

claim: In the open state the anchor domain transitions to a deeper location in the outer leaflet of the bilayer while it tilts and moves away from the permeation pathway.
source: This suggests that in the open state the anchor domain transitions to a deeper location in the outer leaflet of the bilayer (most likely as an extension of TM1), while it tilts and moves away from the permeation pathway (as seen in the MscS expanded conformations, Lai et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on EPR data and comparison with expanded structures.

claim: The typical yield of MscS is about 5-8mg per liter of E. coli.
source: The typical yield of MscS is about 5-8mg per liter of E. coli.
evidence: This is a reported experimental outcome from the purification protocol.

claim: Typical yield of MscS-Cryst is less than 0.1mg per liter of MJF465 E. coli.
source: Typical yield of MscS-Cryst is less than 0.1mg per liter of MJF465 E. coli.
evidence: This is a reported experimental outcome from the purification protocol.

claim: The molar ratio of MscS:MSP1 E3D1:Lipids was 7:10:650 after extensive optimizations.
source: The molar ratio of MscS:MSP1 E3D1:Lipids was 7:10:650, respectively, after extensive optimizations.
evidence: This describes the optimized experimental conditions for nanodisc reconstitution.

claim: The anchor domain is largely present in Enterobacteriales MscS homologs.
source: Comparing the sequences of MscS homologs revealed that this particular structural motif is largely present in Enterobacteriales (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and sequence analysis.

claim: The high resolution 5AJI expanded crystal structure does not show either hook or pore lipids.
source: However, the high resolution 5AJI expanded crystal structure does not show either lipids, which might be due to the lipid being solubilized away in the detergent environment when not protected by the closed conformational N-terminal loop.
evidence: This is based on analysis of a previously published crystal structure with speculation about the reason.

claim: About 70% of alanine substitutions in the anchor domain displayed LOF phenotypes, 8 of those severe.
source: The effect of alanine substitutions was dramatic. About 70% of the mutants displayed LOF phenotypes, 8 of those severe (E2A, V6A, S9A, G12A, N20A, Q21A, L24A, L25A).
evidence: This is based on systematic mutagenesis and functional assays.

claim: Almost a third of cysteine substitutions in the anchor domain display a noticeable LOF phenotype.
source: In fact, an earlier cysteine scan of the same region (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) (Vásquez et al., 2008), shows that almost a third of the mutants display a noticeable LOF phenotype (V7C, N11C, A13C, V18C, and L25C), two were severe (V6C and A19C)
evidence: This is based on previous mutagenesis data, supported by citation.

claim: Most LOF mutations from alanine and cysteine scans map to the subunit interface.
source: and most map to the subunit interface.
evidence: This is based on mapping mutagenesis data onto the structure.

claim: The quality of the density of the anchor domain is significantly degraded in the absence of the N-terminal Hisx6 tag.
source: Interestingly, the quality of the density of the anchor domain is significantly degraded in the absence of the N-terminal Hisx6 tag (Figure 3, left-center), presumably due to an increase in local dynamics in the absence of the stabilizing His-tag.
evidence: This is based on comparison of cryo-EM maps with and without the His-tag.

claim: The hydrophobic mismatch is the main contributing factor in change in the free energy level across different reaction coordinates.
source: Hydrophobic mismatch is the main contributing factor in change in the free energy level across different reaction coordinates.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of different energetic contributions.

claim: The minima in the free energy obtained from MD simulation is matched with that obtained from mean-field calculations at Z distance ~25 Å.
source: Although the hydrophobic mismatch in our initial MD-PMF simulations was not systematically changed (the reaction coordinate was set to move the protein up/down across the bilayer thickness), the minima in the free energy obtained from our MD simulation is matched with that obtained from our mean-field calculations (at the reaction coordinate for the PMF calculations has been defined as the distance between the Z coordinate of the center mass of phosphate molecules of the lipid bilayer and the Z coordinate of center mass of the pore-forming helices of MscS (i.e. residue 105 to 115), Z distance ~25 Å).
evidence: This is based on comparison of different computational approaches.
